title.en: The Heir Sold for Peace: Titu Cusi Hualpa Stolen at Eight Years Old
title.zh: 以嗣子換和平:八歲的圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕遭擄

region.zh: 瓦伊利亞坎的保羅鎮(米科坎恰)(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 20, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Those of Huayllacan had already promised to give Mama Micay, who was their countrywoman and very beautiful, in marriage to Tocay Ccapac, Sinchi of the Ayamarcas their neighbours. When the Ayamarcas saw that the Huayllacans had broken their word they were furious and declared war. While this war was being waged Mama Micay gave birth to her son Titu Cusi Hualpa. Both sides, seeing that they were destroying each other, agreed to come to terms: the Ayamarcas, who were the most powerful, requested those of Huayllacan to deliver the child Titu Cusi Hualpa into their hands, to do what they liked with him; on this condition they would desist from further hostilities. The Huayllacans, fearing this, accepted the condition, although they were uncles and relations of the child. To comply it was necessary to deceive the Inca: a brother of Inca Rocca, named Inca Paucar, asked Inca Rocca to send his nephew to his town of Paulo, that while still a child he might learn to know and care for his relations on his mother's side, who wanted to make him the heir of their estates. Believing these words, the Inca consented. When the child was in their town the Huayllacans made great feasts in honour of Titu Cusi Hualpa, who was then eight years old, his father having sent Incas to guard him. When the festivities were over, the Huayllacans sent to give notice to the Ayamarcas that, while they were occupied in ploughing their chacaras, they might come down on the town and carry off the child. The Ayamarcas came, and finding the child Titu Cusi Hualpa alone, carried it off; all the orejones who had come as a guard from Cuzco were slain.
summary.zh: 瓦伊利亞坎人早先把族中美貌女子瑪瑪·米卡伊許配給鄰邦阿亞馬爾卡之辛奇托卡伊·卡帕克;後來違約另嫁印加·羅卡,阿亞馬爾卡人憤然宣戰。戰火之中,瑪瑪·米卡伊產子圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕。兩邦相持數年,見彼此損耗殆盡,遂議和約——強大的阿亞馬爾卡人提出:交出圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕,任憑發落,否則戰至滅絕。瓦伊利亞坎人雖是孩子的舅家,懼於兵威,竟允其所請。為履行條約,必先誆騙印加王:印加·羅卡之弟印加·保卡爾遣使,請王將幼侄送至自己的保羅鎮,「好讓孩子自幼認識母族親人,繼承他們的家業」。印加·羅卡信以為真,允子前往。孩子入鎮,瓦伊利亞坎人大擺宴席——其時圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕年方八歲,其父另派印加衛士隨行護衛。宴罷,瓦伊利亞坎人密報阿亞馬爾卡人:趁他們下田耕作之際,可入鎮劫走孩子。阿亞馬爾卡人依約而至,見孩子獨處,便將他擄走;自庫斯科前來護衛的耳垂貴胄盡數被殺。

sensitivity.note: The child-kidnapping origin of the Yahuar-huaccac name; kinship betrayal at the heart of the succession myth.

passages.text: It has been related how the Inca Rocca married Mama Micay by the rites of their religion. But it must be understood that those of Huayllacan had already promised to give Mama Micay, who was their countrywoman and very beautiful, in marriage to Tocay Ccapac, Sinchi of the Ayamarcas their neighbours. When the Ayamarcas saw that the Huayllacans had broken their word, they were furious and declared war, considering them as enemies. War was carried on... both sides committing cruelties, inflicting deaths and losses, and causing great injury to each other. While this war was being waged, Mama Micay gave birth to her son Titu Cusi Hualpa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 20 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Ayamarcas, who were the most powerful, requested those of Huayllacan to deliver the child Titu Cusi Hualpa into their hands, to do what they liked with him. On this condition they would desist from further hostilities, but if it was not complied with, they announced that they would continue a mortal war to the end. The Huayllacans, fearing this, and knowing their inability for further resistance, accepted the condition, although they were uncles and relations of the child. In order to comply it was necessary for them to deceive the Inca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 20 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was, in the town of Paulo, a brother of Inca Rocca and uncle of Titu Cusi Hualpa named Inca Paucar. He went or sent messengers to ask Inca Rocca to think well of sending his nephew Titu Cusi Hualpa to his town of Paulo in order that, while still a child, he might learn to know and care for his relations on his mother's side, while they wanted to make him the heir of their estates. Believing in these words the Inca Rocca consented... As soon as they had the child in their town the Huayllacans made great feasts in honour of Titu Cusi Hualpa, who was then eight years old. When the festivities were over, the Huayllacans sent to give notice to the Ayamarcas that, while they were occupied in ploughing certain lands which they call chacaras, they might come down on the town and carry off the child. The Ayamarcas, being informed, came at the time and to the place notified and, finding the child Titu Cusi Hualpa alone, they carried it off.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 20 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Tears of Blood: The Child's Curse on Tocay Ccapac
title.zh: 泣血之咒:幼童對托卡伊·卡帕克的詛咒

region.zh: 阿亞馬爾卡之阿瓦伊羅-坎恰(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 21, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Ayamarcas presented the child Titu Cusi Hualpa to Tocay Ccapac at the chief place of their province called Ahuayro-cancha, saying: 'Look here, Tocay Ccapac, at the prisoner we have brought you.' The Sinchi received his prize with great satisfaction, asking in a loud voice if this was the child of Mama Micay, who ought to have been his wife. Titu Cusi Hualpa, though but a child, replied boldly that he was the son of Mama Micay and of the Inca Rocca. Tocay was indignant when he had heard those words, and ordered those who brought the child as a prisoner to take him out and kill him. The boy, when he heard such a sentence passed upon him, was so filled with sadness and fright that he began to weep from fear of death. He began to shed tears of blood and with indignation beyond his years, in the form of a malediction he said to Tocay and the Ayamarcas: 'I tell you that as sure as you murder me there will come such a curse on you and your descendants that you will all come to an end, without any memory being left of your nation.' The Ayamarcas and Tocay attentively considered this curse of the child together with the tears of blood. They thought there was some great mystery that so young a child should utter such weighty words... They were in suspense divining what it portended. They revoked the sentence of death, calling the child Yahuar-huaccac, which means 'weeper of blood', in allusion to what had taken place. But although they did not wish to kill him then and with their own hands, they ordered that he should lead such a life as that he would die of hunger; they all said to the child that he should turn his face to Cuzco and weep over it, because those curses he had pronounced would fall on the inhabitants of Cuzco, and so it happened.
summary.zh: 阿亞馬爾卡人把圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕押到本省重鎮阿瓦伊羅-坎恰,獻與托卡伊·卡帕克:「瞧,托卡伊·卡帕克,我們給你帶來了俘虜!」辛奇大喜,高聲喝問:這可是本該嫁我的瑪瑪·米卡伊之子?孩子雖幼,卻昂然答道:我是瑪瑪·米卡伊與印加·羅卡之子!托卡伊聞言大怒,喝令將孩子拖出去處死。幼童聞此死刑判決,悲懼交加,竟泣出鮮血;又以超越年齡的憤慨,向托卡伊與阿亞馬爾卡人發出詛咒:「我告訴你們:你們若殺我,咒詛必臨到你們和你們的子孫——你們將滅絕殆盡,你們的國族將無人記起!」托卡伊與眾人反覆思量這孩子的泣血與詛咒:如此年幼竟出此重話,怕是藏著什麼天大的奧秘,便猜度這是否預兆此子將成大器。死刑遂被撤回;眾人因這件事稱他為「亞瓦爾-瓦卡克」——泣血者。他們雖不親手殺他,卻下令讓他過一種終將餓死的生活;臨行又對孩子說:把臉轉向庫斯科,對著它哭吧——你口中的詛咒,將應驗在庫斯科人身上。後來果然如此。

sensitivity.note: The name-giving curse episode; the tears of blood prefigure the dynastic bloodshed of the civil war.

passages.text: The Sinchi received his prize with great satisfaction, asking in a loud voice if this was the child of Mama Micay, who ought to have been his wife. Titu Cusi Hualpa, though but a child, replied boldly that he was the son of Mama Micay and of the Inca Rocca. Tocay was indignant when he had heard those words, and ordered those who brought the child as a prisoner to take him out and kill him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 21 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy, when he heard such a sentence passed upon him, was so filled with sadness and fright, that he began to weep from fear of death. He began to shed tears of blood and with indignation beyond his years, in the form of a malediction he said to Tocay and the Ayamarcas: 'I tell you that as sure as you murder me there will come such a curse on you and your descendants that you will all come to an end, without any memory being left of your nation.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 21 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Ayamarcas and Tocay attentively considered this curse of the child together with the tears of blood. They thought there was some great mystery that so young a child should utter such weighty words, and that the fear of death should make such an impression on him that he should shed tears of blood. They were in suspense divining what it portended, whether that the child would become a great man. They revoked the sentence of death, calling the child Yahuar-huaccac, which means 'weeper of blood', in allusion to what had taken place. Before this they all said to the child that he should turn his face to Cuzco and weep over it, because those curses he had pronounced, would fall on the inhabitants of Cuzco, and so it happened.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Chimpu Orma and the Race to the Hill: The Prince Freed by Anta
title.zh: 欽普·奧爾瑪與登山之賽:安塔人救出王子

region.en: Anta, three leagues from Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科三萊格外的安塔(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 22, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The child Yahuar-huaccac was a year among the shepherds without leaving their huts, which served as a prison, well watched by the shepherds and other guards. But it so happened that there was a woman in the place called Chimpu Orma, native of the town of Anta, three leagues from Cuzco: she was a concubine of the Sinchi Tocay Ccapac, and for this reason she had leave to walk about and go into all parts as she pleased. She was the daughter of the Sinchi of Anta, and having given an account of the treatment of the child to her father, brothers, and relations, she persuaded them to help in his liberation. They came on a certain day and, with the pass given them by Chimpu Orma, arranged the escape. They stationed themselves behind a hill. Yahuar-huaccac was to run in a race with some other boys, to see which could get to the top of the hill first. When the prince reached the top, the men of Anta, who were hidden there, took him in their arms and ran swiftly with him to Anta. When the other boys saw this they quickly gave notice to the valiant guards, who ran after the men of Anta and overtook them at the lake of Huaypon, where there was a fierce battle; finally the Ayamarcas got the worst of it, for they were nearly all killed or wounded. In the town of Anta the boy remained a year, served with much love, but so secretly that his father did not know that he had escaped. At the end of a year those of Anta sent messengers to Inca Rocca; not feeling quite certain of the truth, he sent a poor man seeking charity to make enquiries at Anta, whether it was all true; the poor man ascertained that the child was certainly liberated, and returned with the news. Presently the Inca sent principal people of Cuzco with presents of gold, silver and cloth to the Antas, asking them to send back his son. The Antas replied that they did not want his presents, that they cared more that Yahuar-huaccac should remain with them; yet if Inca Rocca wanted his son he should be returned on condition that, from that time forwards, the Antas should be called relations of the orejones. Inca Rocca conceded what they asked, and brought his son to Cuzco, nominating him successor.
summary.zh: 亞瓦爾-瓦卡克被囚於牧人小屋整整一年,牧人與衛士嚴密看守,無人知其下落。其時營地有一女子,名欽普·奧爾瑪,乃庫斯科三萊格外安塔鎮人——托卡伊·卡帕克的妾,因此得以自由行走四方。她是安塔辛奇之女;她把幼童的遭遇告知父親、兄弟與親族,勸他們相助營救。某日,他們持欽普·奧爾瑪給的通行之權前來,預伏於一座山後。約定:亞瓦爾-瓦卡克將與其他男孩賽跑,看誰先登頂。王子一到山頂,潛伏的安塔人便將他攔腰抱起,飛奔而回安塔。同伴孩童見狀急報衛士;衛士狂追,在瓦伊蓬湖追上安塔人,一場惡戰——阿亞馬爾卡人幾乎全軍覆沒。王子在安塔鎮安居一年,備受愛戴,但行事極其隱秘,連其父印加·羅卡也不知他已脫身。一年之後,安塔人遣使報信;印加·羅卡尚不敢盡信,又派一名化緣的窮人往安塔查證。窮人證實王子確已獲釋,回報庫斯科,舉城再慶。印加王隨即遣重臣攜金銀布帛贈安塔人,求還其子。安塔人卻答:禮物不必了,他們更願意亞瓦爾-瓦卡克留居安塔,好讓他們侍奉王子父子;若印加王執意索回,須應一條件——自此以後,安塔人得稱為「耳垂貴胄」的親戚。印加·羅卡親赴安塔,允其所請,攜子回庫斯科,立為儲君。

sensitivity.note: The rescue that founded the Anta-Cuzco kinship pact - a founding charter narrated through a children's race.

Yahuar-huaccac was to run in a race with some other boys, to see which could get to the top of the hill first. When the prince reached the top, the men of Anta, who were hidden there, took him in their arms and ran swiftly with him to Anta. The poor man went, ascertained that the child was certainly liberated, and returned with the news to Inca Rocca... Presently the Inca sent many principal people of Cuzco with presents of gold, silver, and cloth to the Antas, asking them to receive them and to send back his son. texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Heir Killed in Paulo Again: The Huayllacans' Second Treason
title.zh: 保羅鎮再演弒儲:瓦伊利亞坎人的二次背叛

region.zh: 瓦伊利亞坎的保羅鎮(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 23, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Yahuar-huaccac had by his wife Mama Chicya three legitimate sons: the eldest Paucar Ayllu; the second Pahuac Hualpa Mayta, chosen to succeed his father though he was not the eldest; the third Viracocha, who was afterwards Inca through the death of his brother. As the Huayllacans wanted Marca-yutu to succeed Yahuar-huaccac, because he was their relation, they determined to kill Pahuac Hualpa Mayta who was nominated to succeed. With this object they asked his father to let him go to Paulo. Forgetting their former treason, he sent the child to its grandfather Soma Inca with forty orejones of the ayllus of Cuzco as his guard. When he came to their town they killed him, for which the Inca, his father, inflicted a great punishment on the Huayllacans, killing some and banishing others until very few were left.
summary.zh: 亞瓦爾-瓦卡克與王后瑪瑪·奇西亞生三個嫡子:長子保卡爾·阿伊柳;次子帕瓜克·瓦爾帕·馬雅塔,雖非長子,卻被立為儲君;三子維拉科查,因兄長遇害而終得大位。瓦伊利亞坎人欲使自己親戚馬爾卡-尤圖繼位,便謀殺儲君帕瓜克·瓦爾帕·馬雅塔。他們請求印加王准孩子前往保羅;印加王忘卻舊恨,竟遣幼子赴外祖父索馬·印加處,並派庫斯科阿伊柳的四十名耳垂貴胄護衛。孩子一到鎮上,他們便將他殺害。印加王大怒,嚴懲瓦伊利亞坎人——或誅或逐,直至其族所剩無幾。

sensitivity.note: The second child-murder in the same town; the repetition is the point - the Huayllacan kinship is twice traitorous in this tradition.

passages.text: As the Huayllacans wanted Marca-yutu to succeed Yahuar-huaccac, because he was their relation, they determined to kill Pahuac Hualpa Mayta, who was nominated to succeed. With this object they asked his father to let him go to Paulo. Forgetting their former treason, he sent the child to its grandfather Soma Inca with forty orejones of the ayllus of Cuzco as his guard. When he came to their town they killed him, for which the Inca, his father, inflicted a great punishment on the Huayllacans, killing some and banishing others until very few were left.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Night Apparition at Urcos: How Hatun Tupac Became Viracocha Inca
title.zh: 烏爾科斯夜現真神:哈頓·圖帕克改名維拉科查

region.en: Urcos, five leagues from Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科五萊格外烏爾科斯(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 24, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Once when Hatun Tupac Inca was in Urcos, a town a little more than five leagues S.S.E. of Cuzco, where there was a sumptuous huaca in honour of Ticci Viracocha, the deity appeared to him in the night. Next morning he assembled his orejones, among them his tutor Hualpa Rimachi, and told them how Viracocha had appeared to him that night, and had announced great good fortune to him and his descendants. In congratulating him Hualpa Rimachi saluted him: 'O Viracocha Inca.' The rest followed his example and celebrated this name, and the Inca retained it all the rest of his life. Others say that he took this name because, when he was armed as a knight and had his ears bored, he took Ticci Viracocha as the godfather of his knighthood. Be it as it may, all that is certain is that when a child, before he succeeded his father, he was named Hatun Tupac Inca, and afterwards, for the rest of his life, Viracocha Inca.
summary.zh: 哈頓·圖帕克·印加行至庫斯科東南偏南五萊格外的烏爾科斯鎮——那裡有一座供奉提基·維拉科查的豪華瓦卡——夜間,神祇向他顯現。次日清晨,他召集耳垂貴胄——其中包括他的師傅瓦爾帕·里馬奇——講述夜間維拉科查顯靈之事,以及神向他與其子孫預許的大福。師傅瓦爾帕·里馬奇賀道:「維拉科查·印加!」眾人隨之歡呼,共賀新名;印加王自此終身用之。另有異說:他之所以取此名,是因受武穿耳之時,拜提基·維拉科查為受武的教父。無論如何,可以確定的是:他繼位之前幼名哈頓·圖帕克·印加,此後終身名維拉科查·印加。

sensitivity.note: Royal theophany and renaming; the king takes the Creator's own name as his regnal title.

passages.text: Once when this Hatun Tupac Inca was in Urcos, a town which is a little more than five leagues S.S.E. of Cuzco, where there was a sumptuous huaca in honour of Ticci Viracocha, the deity appeared to him in the night. Next morning he assembled his orejones, among them his tutor Hualpa Rimachi, and told them how Viracocha had appeared to him that night, and had announced great good fortune to him and his descendants.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 24 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: In congratulating him Hualpa Rimachi saluted him, 'O Viracocha Inca.' The rest followed his example and celebrated this name, and the Inca retained it all the rest of his life. Others say that he took this name, because, when he was armed as a knight and had his ears bored, he took Ticci Viracocha as the godfather of his knighthood. Be it as it may, all that is certain is that when a child, before he succeeded his father, he was named Hatun Tupac Inca, and afterwards, for the rest of his life, Viracocha Inca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 24 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Old King Flees to Xaquixaguana: Gonzalo Pizarro Burns the Body
title.zh: 老王遁走夏基夏瓜納:皮薩羅焚屍索金

region.zh: 卡基亞-夏基夏瓜納(薩克薩瓦納)(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 25, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: As Viracocha was now very old, he nominated as his successor his bastard son Inca Urco, without regard to the order of succession, because he was very fond of his mother. This Inca was bold, proud, and despised others, so that he aroused the indignation of the warriors, more especially of the legitimate sons, and of the valiant captains Apu Mayta and Vicaquirau. These took order to prevent this succession, secretly setting their eyes on the third of the legitimate sons named Cusi, afterwards called Inca Yupanqui, because they believed that he was mild and affable, and showed signs of high spirit and lofty ideas. While they were consulting how it should be managed, the Chancas of Andahuaylas marched upon that city. Inca Viracocha, from fear of them, fled from Cuzco, and went to a place called Caquia Xaquixahuana, where he shut himself up, being afraid of the Chancas. Here he died after some years, deprived of Cuzco, of which his son Cusi had possession for several years before his father's death. This Inca was industrious, and inventor of cloths and embroidered work called Viracocha-tocapu, and amongst us brocade. He was buried in Caquia Xaquixahuana, and Gonzalo Pizarro, having heard that there was treasure with the body, discovered it and a large sum of gold; he burnt the body, and the natives collected the ashes and hid them in a vase. This, with the Inca's guauqui called Inca Amaru, was found by the Licentiate Polo, when he was Corregidor of Cuzco.
summary.zh: 維拉科查年事已高,不按繼位次序,竟立寵妃之子、庶出的印加·烏爾庫為儲。烏爾庫驕横傲慢,輕視他人,激起武人——尤其是嫡子們與猛將阿普·馬雅塔、維卡基勞——的憤慨。他們密謀阻止這樁繼承,暗中屬意三子庫西(即後來的印加·尤潘琪),因他溫和可親,又顯露出高遠之志。正當他們謀劃之際,安達瓦伊利亞斯的昌卡人進逼庫斯科。維拉科查懼敵,棄城而逃,退至卡基亞-夏基夏瓜納,閉門自守;數年後客死於斯,庫斯科早已在其子庫西手中。這位印加王勤於制作,是「維拉科查-托卡普」織金錦緞的發明者。他葬於夏基夏瓜納;貢薩洛·皮薩羅聞說隨葬有寶,掘墓得大批黃金,竟將遺體焚毀。土人收拾骨灰,藏於甕中;連同這位印加王的瓜烏基「印加·阿瑪魯」,一併被後來任庫斯科行政長官的波羅先生尋獲。

sensitivity.note: The flight that opened the way for Pachacuti; the body-burning by Pizarro is the conquest's violation of the ancestor cult.
